Fermat's Last Theorem. It states that for any integer n greater than two, there exist no three positive integers x, y, z such that x to the n plus y to the n equals z to the n. Pierre de Fermat claimed, without proof, to have solved this around sixteen thirty-seven, triggering a three hundred fifty-eight year mathematical odyssey. Andrew Wiles finally proved it in nineteen ninety-five using elliptic curves and modular forms, a deep connection no one anticipated. The theorem exemplifies how a simple-to-state problem can unlock vast new mathematics.

Fermat claimed a proof in the margin of Diophantus' Arithmetica but left no details. He wrote, "I have a truly marvelous proof, but this margin is too small." For n equals two, the equation x squared plus y squared equals z squared has infinitely many solutions, like the Pythagorean triples three-four-five and five-twelve-thirteen. No integer solutions exist for n greater than or equal to three, making the jump qualitative and profound.

Leonhard Euler proved the case n equals three in the eighteenth century, using infinite descent. He also proved n equals four. Sophie Germain proved infinitely many cases through deep number-theoretic arguments in the nineteenth century. Wiles' nineteen ninety-five proof, after seven years of secret work, established a link between elliptic curves and modular forms. It proved the Taniyama-Shimura conjecture, which immediately implied Fermat's Last Theorem.

The Taniyama-Shimura conjecture, proposed by Yutaka Taniyama, Goro Shimura, and others, stated that every rational elliptic curve is modular. Proving this seemed impossibly hard before Wiles' insight. Wiles' proof required over one hundred pages of dense algebraic geometry and introduced techniques, especially modularity lifting theorems, that revolutionized arithmetic geometry and number theory. The proof uses deformation theory, Galois representations, and deep results from the theory of automorphic forms. This machinery only became available in the late twentieth century.

Fermat's Last Theorem stands as a monument to mathematical obstinacy: the simplest-to-state hard problem in number theory, solved only through techniques that post-date Fermat by more than three hundred fifty years. The theorem's resolution illustrates how seemingly isolated problems can connect deep mathematical structures, opening entire new fields of research.
